_sources.usda: USDA FoodData Central, https://fdc.nal.usda.gov/ (record named in each entry), read 2026-10-27
_sources.nihOds: NIH Office of Dietary Supplements fact sheets (Iron, Folate, Vitamin C, Vitamin K, Magnesium, Zinc, Potassium, Vitamin A, Calcium, Vitamin B12, Vitamin D, Vitamin E), https://ods.od.nih.gov/factsheets/list-all/; reference intakes as listed in build_draft_batch.py (RDA for adult women)
_sources.niddk: NIDDK, Eating, Diet & Nutrition for Kidney Stones, read 2026-10-26: nuts and nut products, peanuts, rhubarb, spinach and wheat bran listed among foods to reduce for calcium oxalate stones

rye.how: Soak, then simmer rye berries until chewy for grain salads and side dishes.
rye.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
rye.reviewNote: The USDA record is dry rye grain. Cooked rye berries absorb water, so a cup of cooked grain has much less per cup. Rye bread, rye flour and rye crackers are separate foods. Contains gluten.
rye.name: Rye

wheat.how: Simmer whole wheat berries until tender for salads and pilafs; soaking first shortens the cooking time.
wheat.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
wheat.reviewNote: The catalogue entry "Wheat" does not say which wheat; USDA's durum wheat grain was used, and hard red or soft wheat berries differ somewhat. Dry, uncooked grain. USDA lists no fibre value for this record, so fibre is not shown. Contains gluten.
wheat.name: Wheat

amaranth.how: Simmer in water until soft and porridge-like, or pop it like popcorn.
amaranth.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
amaranth.reviewNote: Cooked amaranth grain; amaranth leaves are a different food. USDA lists no folate, vitamin A, C or K values for this record.
amaranth.name: Amaranth

millet.how: Simmer until fluffy for side dishes, porridge, or in place of rice.
millet.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
millet.name: Millet

bagel.desc: Bagels, plain, enriched, with calcium propionate (includes onion, poppy, sesame)
bagel.how: Toast and top with eggs, avocado, cheese or nut butter.
bagel.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
bagel.reviewNote: Plain enriched bagel; whole-grain and flavoured bagels differ. Iron and folate come largely from enrichment. A medium bagel is about 275 kcal and is a large serving of refined grain.
bagel.name: Bagel

couscous.how: Steep in hot water or stock, fluff with a fork, and add vegetables, beans or herbs.
couscous.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
couscous.reviewNote: Standard (semolina) couscous, which is a wheat pasta and contains gluten; whole-wheat and pearl (Israeli) couscous differ.
couscous.name: Couscous

egg-noodles.how: Boil briefly, then add to soups, stir-fries or serve with sauce and vegetables.
egg-noodles.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
egg-noodles.reviewNote: Enriched egg noodles, cooked; folate and iron come mainly from enrichment. Contain egg and wheat.
egg-noodles.name: Egg noodles

granola.how: Spoon over yoghurt or fruit, or eat with milk; a small portion goes a long way because it is calorie-dense.
granola.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
granola.reviewNote: USDA's homemade granola. Shop-bought granola varies a lot (many contain much more sugar), so the numbers are a rough guide only. A typical bowlful is much more than 1 oz.
granola.name: Granola

naan.desc: Bread, naan, plain, commercially prepared, refrigerated
naan.how: Warm and serve with curries, dals and dips, or use as a base for flatbread toppings.
naan.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
naan.reviewNote: Commercial plain naan; restaurant naan often contains butter or ghee and differs. USDA lists no folate, vitamin A, C or K values for this record.
naan.name: Naan

pasta.desc: Pasta, cooked, enriched, without added salt
pasta.how: Boil until al dente and toss with vegetables, beans, olive oil or sauce.
pasta.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
pasta.reviewNote: Regular enriched wheat pasta, cooked. Folate and iron come largely from enrichment. Whole-wheat pasta is a separate profile.
pasta.name: Pasta

pita-bread.how: Warm and fill with salad and protein, or cut into wedges for dips.
pita-bread.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
pita-bread.name: Pita bread (whole-wheat)

polenta.how: Whisk into simmering water or stock until thick and creamy, then top with vegetables, cheese or beans.
polenta.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
polenta.reviewNote: Dry whole-grain cornmeal. Polenta is cooked with several times its weight in water, so one cooked cup has far less per cup. Degermed (more common) cornmeal has less fibre and minerals.
polenta.name: Polenta / cornmeal

popcorn.how: Air-pop and season lightly with herbs or a little oil and salt.
popcorn.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
popcorn.reviewNote: Plain air-popped popcorn. Microwave and cinema popcorn have butter, oil and salt added, which this record does not show.
popcorn.name: Popcorn (plain)

rice-cakes.desc: Snacks, rice cakes, brown rice, plain, unsalted
rice-cakes.how: Top with nut butter, avocado, cottage cheese or hummus.
rice-cakes.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
rice-cakes.reviewNote: Plain brown-rice cakes; flavoured and white-rice versions differ.
rice-cakes.name: Rice cakes

rice-noodles.how: Soak or boil as the packet says, then add to soups, stir-fries and salads.
rice-noodles.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
rice-noodles.reviewNote: Plain cooked rice noodles; they are naturally wheat-free but labels vary.
rice-noodles.name: Rice noodles

rye-bread.how: Toast and top with eggs, fish, cheese or vegetables, or use for sandwiches.
rye-bread.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
rye-bread.reviewNote: Commercial US rye bread, which is often part wheat; a dense 100% rye loaf differs. Contains gluten.
rye-bread.name: Rye bread

soba-noodles.how: Boil briefly, rinse, and serve cold with a dipping sauce or hot in broth.
soba-noodles.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
soba-noodles.reviewNote: USDA lists no fibre value. Many soba noodles are part wheat; 100% buckwheat soba is different, and wheat content matters for gluten.
soba-noodles.name: Soba noodles

sourdough-bread.portion: 2 oz of sliced bread (USDA: 1 oz = 28.35 g)
sourdough-bread.how: Toast and top with eggs, avocado or beans, or serve with soups and salads.
sourdough-bread.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
sourdough-bread.reviewNote: USDA groups sourdough with French and Vienna bread in one record; an artisan sourdough loaf may differ. Contains gluten; no claim is made about fermentation, digestion or blood sugar.
sourdough-bread.name: Sourdough bread

tortillas.desc: Tortillas, ready-to-bake or -fry, flour, shelf stable
tortillas.how: Warm and fill with beans, vegetables, eggs or meat, or bake into wraps and quesadillas.
tortillas.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
tortillas.reviewNote: Flour (wheat) tortilla; corn tortillas are a different food. Sizes vary a lot.
tortillas.name: Tortillas (wheat)

wheat-flour.desc: Wheat flour, whole-grain (Includes foods for USDA's Food Distribution Program)
wheat-flour.how: Use in baking, pancakes and flatbreads, often combined with white flour for a lighter texture.
wheat-flour.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
wheat-flour.reviewNote: Dry flour, as an ingredient; values apply to the flour, not to the finished baked goods.
wheat-flour.name: Wheat flour (whole-grain)

white-rice.desc: Rice, white, long-grain, regular, enriched, cooked
white-rice.how: Rinse, then simmer until tender, and serve with vegetables, beans, fish or meat.
white-rice.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
white-rice.reviewNote: Enriched white rice; folate and iron come largely from enrichment. Brown, basmati and sushi rice are separate foods.
white-rice.name: White rice

whole-wheat-pasta.desc: Pasta, whole-wheat, cooked (Includes foods for USDA's Food Distribution Program)
whole-wheat-pasta.how: Boil until just tender and toss with vegetables, beans or a simple sauce.
whole-wheat-pasta.evidence: Nutrient amounts and reference intakes only (USDA FoodData Central, NIH ODS).
whole-wheat-pasta.name: Whole-wheat pasta
